passages.t: Eyes on God when no one knows what to do
passages.happening:
‘After this, the Moabites and Ammonites, together with some of the Meunites, came to make war against Jehoshaphat’ (verse 1). A vast army is already at En-gedi (verse 2). ‘Jehoshaphat was alarmed and set his face to seek the LORD. And he proclaimed a fast throughout Judah’ (verse 3), and people come from every city to seek him (verse 4).

Standing in the assembly at the temple, Jehoshaphat prays, “O LORD, God of our fathers, are You not the God who is in heaven, and do You not rule over all the kingdoms of the nations? Power and might are in Your hand, and no one can stand against You” (verse 6). He recalls the land God gave and the promise of the temple, that in disaster they would stand before this house and cry out and God would hear (verses 7-9). He names the invaders, whom Israel had spared on the way from Egypt (verses 10-11), and ends, “We do not know what to do, but our eyes are upon You” (verse 12). ‘Meanwhile all the men of Judah, with their wives and children and little ones, were standing before the LORD’ (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
Rebuked and reformed, Jehoshaphat now faces his greatest test. The chapter is one of the most loved in Chronicles because it shows a king and a people doing exactly what Solomon's prayer and God's answer in 7:14 described: in distress they gather, humble themselves, seek the LORD, and are heard.

The invaders came from east and south of the Dead Sea: Moab to the east, Ammon to the north-east, and the Meunites from near Edom. The traditional Hebrew of verse 2 reads Aram; the BSB and many translations read Edom, a difference of one similar letter, and the geography favors Edom. En-gedi was an oasis on the western shore of the Dead Sea, so the army was climbing into Judah's wilderness south-east of Jerusalem. The invasion is not recorded in Kings. Moab had been subject to Israel under Ahab, and King Mesha's own inscription, the Moabite Stone found in 1868, boasts of throwing off Israel's rule; many place this chapter in the unsettled years after Ahab's death, though the link is uncertain.

A public fast, tsom, was the whole community humbling itself in a crisis. Everyone gathered, children too. The prayer moves from God's rule over the nations, to the gift of the land, to the promise attached to the temple, to the present danger, to a confession of helplessness. Israel had been forbidden to attack Ammon, Moab and Edom on the way from Egypt, so the invasion is told as ingratitude.
passages.later: Solomon had prayed for this day: ‘and when they pray in the direction of the land that You gave to their fathers’ (2 Chronicles 6:38). A psalm says, ‘I lift up my eyes to the hills. From where does my help come?’ (Psalm 121:1).
passages.asks: Jehoshaphat told God that he did not know what to do, but that his eyes were on him. Ask where you do not know what to do right now. And ask whether you could pray that prayer honestly, with your family standing beside you.

passages.happening:
The Spirit of the LORD comes on Jahaziel, a Levite of Asaph's line (verse 14): “Do not be afraid or discouraged because of this vast army, for the battle does not belong to you, but to God” (verse 15). ‘You need not fight this battle. Take up your positions, stand firm, and see the salvation of the LORD on your behalf’ (verse 17). The king and the people bow down, and the Levites praise God with a loud voice (verses 18-19).

In the morning Jehoshaphat says, “Believe in the LORD your God, and you will be upheld; believe in His prophets, and you will succeed” (verse 20). He appoints singers to go before the army, singing, “Give thanks to the LORD, for His loving devotion endures forever” (verse 21). ‘The moment they began their shouts and praises, the LORD set ambushes against the men of Ammon, Moab, and Mount Seir’ (verse 22), and the invaders turn on one another (verse 23). Judah gathers the spoil for three days and assembles in the Valley of Beracah to praise the LORD (verses 25-26), and returns to Jerusalem with harps, lyres and trumpets (verses 27-28). ‘Then Jehoshaphat’s kingdom was at peace, for his God had given him rest on every side’ (verse 30).
passages.hearers:
Jahaziel's word answers each fear, repeating do not be afraid or discouraged, and echoes Moses at the Red Sea: stand firm and see the salvation of the LORD. Verse 20 plays on one root, aman: believe and you will be made firm, or upheld. The procession turns the battle into worship. The singers go first, and the victory begins the moment they praise. They sing the refrain of Psalm 136, sung at the temple's dedication, praising God's loving devotion, chesed.

The singers came from the Levite families David had appointed to lead worship. The valley's name, Beracah, comes from the praise they gave there, and naming a place for an event was a common way to keep its memory. The story circles back from the valley to the temple with music and ends with rest.
passages.later: Moses had said at the Red Sea, ‘Do not be afraid. Stand firm and you will see the LORD’s salvation, which He will accomplish for you today’ (Exodus 14:13). Isaiah used the same play on words: ‘If you do not stand firm in your faith, then you will not stand at all’ (Isaiah 7:9).
passages.hard:
Does this chapter teach that God's people should expect miraculous victories if they pray and praise? And what of the armies destroying one another?

The chapter shows God answering a particular prayer in a particular way, and it holds up Judah's trust as a model. It does not promise that every threat will be removed by praise. Chronicles itself records faithful people who suffered, and the wider Bible, from the psalms of lament to the persecution of the apostles, shows that God's faithfulness does not always look like escape. Some readers stress the power of worship and prayer and draw from it bold expectation of God's help. Others stress that the main point is the posture of dependence, which God honors whether or not rescue comes in the form asked. Both agree that the chapter calls God's people to seek him first in a crisis and to trust that the outcome is his.

The invaders' destruction is told in a single verse, as a confusion that turned their own swords on one another. The text gives it as God's doing in defense of a people who did not lift a weapon, and it does not linger. It is not a pattern for how God's people should treat anyone.
passages.asks: The singers went out ahead of the army. Ask what it would look like to praise God before you see how a hard thing will end. And ask what battle you have been fighting that God may be telling you is not yours.

passages.t: Jehoshaphat's reign, and one more alliance
passages.happening:
Jehoshaphat reigns twenty-five years in Jerusalem and walks in the way of his father Asa, doing what is right (verses 31-32). ‘The high places, however, were not removed; the people had not yet set their hearts on the God of their fathers’ (verse 33). His acts are written in the records of Jehu son of Hanani (verse 34).

‘Later, Jehoshaphat king of Judah made an alliance with Ahaziah king of Israel, who acted wickedly’ (verse 35). They build ships at Ezion-geber to go to Tarshish (verse 36). The prophet Eliezer says, “Because you have allied yourself with Ahaziah, the LORD has destroyed your works” (verse 37), and the ships are wrecked.
passages.hearers:
The chapter ends honestly. The unremoved high places sit awkwardly beside 17:6, where Jehoshaphat removed them; the difference may be between what the king did and what the people did, since the people had not yet set their hearts on God. And Jehoshaphat, after everything, joins the north again. The verb join, chavar, comes three times in the closing verses. Tarshish ships were large trading vessels for long voyages.

First Kings 22 also tells of the ships wrecked at Ezion-geber, at the north end of the Gulf of Aqaba, and says that Jehoshaphat afterward refused Ahaziah's request to join him. The two accounts can be read as describing different stages of the venture. The next chapter shows what the alliance with Ahab's house produced in his son.
passages.later: First Kings says, ‘Jehoshaphat built ships of Tarshish to go to Ophir for gold, but they never set sail, because they were wrecked at Ezion-geber’ (1 Kings 22:48).
passages.asks: Even after the great victory, Jehoshaphat made the same kind of alliance again. Ask which old pattern you keep returning to after God has delivered you from its results. And ask what it would take to set your heart, and not only your habits, on God.
